title: Dedicated vs Hosted architecture performance review
summary: Phone screen / technical deep dive to compare Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted for Voltara's inference workloads. Focus on isolation, noisy neighbor risks, throughput guarantees, KV cache behavior, batching and quantization trade-offs, VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a 2-week dedicated pilot benchmark and to exchange security docs and benchmark template.
action_items: Carlos Nguyen (SE): Share benchmark spreadsheet + kernel-level perf counters (due: 2025-03-17)
Maya Patel (AE): Send Dedicated pricing tier + example SLA language (due: 2025-03-14)
Dev Singh (Customer): Provide representative prompt set and 48-hour token distribution (due: 2025-03-18)
Hannah Cho (Customer): Request security questionnaire answers and KMS integration checklist (due: 2025-03-16)
next_steps: Schedule 1 week baseline hosted vs dedicated perf run (Carlos to coordinate)
Redwood to provision dedicated pool for 2-week pilot once test data received
Share secure link to security docs and SOC2 report
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Lisa (Voltara Infra), Dev (Voltara ML), Hannah (Voltara Security)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros — I'm Maya, I'm the account lead, and Carlos is our solutions engineer who's going to drive the performance bits.
[00:12] Carlos (Redwood): Hi all. Quick agenda: isolation vs noisy neighbor, latency vs throughput tradeoffs, kv cache and batching behavior, quantization notes, and VPC/on-prem caveats. Then open Q&A and next steps.
[00:28] Lisa (Voltara): Sounds good. We're trying to understand whether Dedicated buys us the isolation and predictable throughput we need for our real-time triage product. We have tight p95 latency targets and strict data residency for PHI.
[00:40] Dev (Voltara): I'll add — our workloads are mixed: short chatty prompts (~20 tokens) for triage and longer summarizations (~1.5k tokens) occasionally. Peak concurrent requests around 300.
[00:53] Hannah (Voltara): And security is key — KMS, SSO, audit logs, that sort of thing. We also need to know how updates are rolled out and whether kernels can be pinned.
[01:05] Carlos (Redwood): Great. On isolation: Dedicated gives you a reserved GPU pool, you get physical isolation at the pool level. That means noisy neighbor risks are essentially eliminated inside the pool — you won't be sharing GPU time with unknown tenants. There are still VM-level services on the host but we segregate inference runtime across tenants.
[01:30] Lisa: When you say "reserved GPU pool" — is that per-customer GPUs pinned, or a soft reservation?
[01:38] Carlos: For Dedicated it's a hard reservation on the GPU cluster for your account for the duration of the contract. We also support soft burst to additional capacity if you've enabled burst. The important bit is scheduling: we don't colocate other customers' workloads on those GPUs.
[01:55] Dev: OK, so noisy neighbor mostly solved. What about throughput guarantees? p50/p95 numbers?
[02:02] Carlos: Throughput guarantees come from a combination of Dedicated capacity sizing and autoscale policy. For p50 you can get very stable numbers — e.g., for a 70B dense model on an A100-ish profile we see p50 token latency of X ms under continuous batching at size Y. I'll share concrete numbers in the spreadsheet — those are kernel and model dependent.
[02:28] Maya: Important: we map to your expected tokens/sec and concurrency to pick pool size. For SLAs, we provide uptime SLAs and latency SLAs for committed capacity tiers.
[02:40] Hannah: Are those latency SLAs tied to specific model versions or sequence lengths? We need to avoid surprises when long traces come through.
[02:48] Carlos: They are defined per-profile and sequence length band. The SLA references a model profile (for example: gpt-open-70b / seq <=1024). We also recommend conservative handling for tail heavy workloads — for example, fallback policies to cheaper model variants for long sequences to preserve throughput.
[03:05] Lisa: Let's dig into KV cache — we're planning heavy use of prefix caching for user sessions. How does Dedicated manage KV cache persistence and eviction?
[03:15] Carlos: Redwood runtime uses a combination of in-GPU KV cache and an optional hot-ram cache for very large session sets. On Dedicated, KV cache is per-tenant within the pool. We expose LRU eviction metrics and a configurable per-connection KV cache size. Eviction behavior depends on memory pressure and sequence lengths — large sequences produce bigger KV footprints.
[03:36] Dev: Is the KV cache wiped on pod restarts? We need TTLs for sessions—cold restart would be bad for p95.
[03:44] Carlos: Good call — we persist in-memory KV while the process stays up. On restarts it's cold; we have warmup techniques: pre-warming via prefetch and pinned KV snapshots you can store in S3 (encrypted) and load at startup. For Dedicated we can do more aggressive warm-warm strategies — e.g., retain warmed containers for sticky sessions.
[04:05] Maya: We'll include recommended pre-warm scripts in the playbook.
[04:11] [Small crosstalk] Dev: That helps.
[04:20] Lisa: Batching — how do you balance latency for short chatty requests vs throughput for long gen jobs?
[04:30] Carlos: We use continuous batching with latency budgets. For short prompts, we recommend a small max-batch size and aggressive latency cutoff (e.g., 8-16ms window) to keep p95 low. For throughput jobs, larger batch sizes amortize kernel overhead. We can route requests by policy — e.g., route short chat to a low-latency pool and heavy batches to a throughput pool, or use model variants with different quantization.
[05:00] Dev: So routing policies are per-route in the API?
[05:04] Maya: Yes, in the Redwood Console you can configure per-route policies, fallbacks, and pin model versions.
[05:12] Hannah: Quantization — quality vs cost. We expect to evaluate int8 or nf4 for some models. What's the expected perf lift and what are the gotchas?
[05:22] Carlos: Quantization depends on model architecture. For many transformer models, int8 or nf4 can reduce memory footprint by ~2-4x and increase throughput significantly because you fit larger batch sizes on the GPU. However, you may see quality regressions on rare tokens or in long-context tasks. We recommend a two-track approach: run evals on your prompt set (we'll help) and use redwood Optimize to suggest the best quant profile. For Dedicated you can pin quantization profiles so rollout is controlled.
[05:55] Lisa: Are kernels auto-selected per quant profile?
[06:00] Carlos: Yes — the runtime has a kernel-selection layer that matches model architecture, quantization, sequence length patterns, and hardware to pick optimal kernels. We also expose low-level perf counters if you want to see flop utilization, memory bandwidth, and cache hit ratios.
[06:20] Dev: Where do we see those perf counters? Is that in Console or via an API stream?
[06:26] Carlos: Both. Console dashboards show aggregated counters and per-route breakdowns. We also stream raw kernel counters to your monitoring endpoint in Prometheus-compatible format if you want to ingest them.
[06:38] Hannah: Networking for VPC/on-prem — we have strict egress limitations. If we run Private (on-prem) do we still need outbound calls to Redwood control plane?
[06:50] Carlos: For Private VPC deployments the control plane can be configured to use a customer-managed endpoint. For fully air-gapped on-prem we provide an offline control plane bundle. For Dedicated in a cloud VPC, you can restrict egress via private endpoints and peering. We'll share the network diagram.
[07:10] Lisa: Great. Also curious about multi-tenant management inside our org — RBAC, audit trails, and key management.
[07:18] Maya: Dedicated supports RBAC and SSO. For KMS, we integrate with customer-managed keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM) for model artifacts and logs encryption. Audit logs are shipped to your audit bucket and retained per policy.
[07:34] Dev: Back to noisy neighbor — hypothetically, if we burst to a shared fleet, is there telemetry that tells us when we're bumped?
[07:44] Carlos: Yes — when bursting into shared capacity we mark requests as best-effort and include a header on responses. The Console has a fallback trace that shows the route used and if any request was executed on burst capacity. For SLAs, only committed capacity is covered; burst is best-effort.
[08:02] Lisa: For throughput guarantees during major incidents we need isolation — is there an option to disable burst entirely?
[08:08] Maya: Absolutely, you can opt out of burst and enforce strict capacity limits. That comes at a cost but gives deterministic throughput.
[08:18] [Pause / background noise]
[08:26] Dev: Can you describe how tail latency behaves with batching? I mean, p95 blips when there is a tail of large sequences.
[08:35] Carlos: Tail latency is typically due to heterogenous sequence lengths and cold cache misses. The runtime addresses this by dynamic batching that groups by sequence length buckets and by prioritizing requests based on latency SLAs. You can set route priority, so short prompts get preemptive scheduling.
[08:56] Dev: Any recommended batch sizes for our mix (20-token chatty vs 1.5k summary)?
[09:03] Carlos: For chatty prompts, max batch 16-32 with latency cutoff ~10-20ms. For long summaries, batch sizes 2-8 depending on memory. We'll recommend a pool mix: dedicate a high-priority low-batch pool for chat and a throughput pool with larger batches for summaries.
[09:22] Lisa: How do model rollouts interact with Dedicated? Can you do canary for new kernels or quantized builds?
[09:30] Carlos: Yes — rollout supports canary and A/B experiments within your Dedicated pool. You can pin a subset of nodes to a canary kernel or quant profile and route a % of traffic. We also support automatic rollback on perf regressions.
[09:45] Hannah: On the security front — what does the audit trail look like for kernel upgrades and who can approve them?
[09:52] Maya: Kernel upgrades are logged as change events with a signed artifact. In Dedicated, customers can choose to approve upgrades via the Console workflow. We keep a changelog and you can lock versions.
[10:05] [Customer asks off-record clarifying question about compliance]
[10:12] Carlos: Quick note on benchmarking: we'll want your prompt distribution and a representative concurrency pattern. We'll run both hosted baseline and dedicated pilot using the same dataset. The spreadsheet we'll send has fields: prompt, expected tokens, sequence length, concurrency pattern, success criteria (p95 latency, throughput per GPU), and quality threshold.
[10:35] Dev: We can provide that. Also we want to run quantized vs fp16 comparisons.
[10:40] Carlos: Perfect. For quantized runs we'll include paired evals and show token-level diffs and perplexity deltas. We also run regeneration checks and hallucination-focused prompts.
[10:56] Lisa: On costs — does Dedicated automatically lower unit cost? Or is it a flat reserved price? We want to understand unit economics for our CFO.
[11:05] Maya: Dedicated is reserved capacity with pricing tiers. Unit cost can be lower because you avoid multi-tenant overhead and you can use quantized profiles to reduce GPU memory and increase throughput. We'll include cost modeling examples in the pricing deck.
[11:20] Dev: Any limitations for model families on Dedicated vs Hosted? For example, do you support certain open models only on Hosted?
[11:28] Carlos: We can support the same catalog across both, but some experimental kernels might be initially gated on Hosted. For production-dedicated we validate kernels and quant builds before enabling them. If you need a specific forked model we can onboard it in dedicated but it goes through a validation run.
[11:46] Hannah: How about disaster recovery — snapshot cadence, KV snapshots, and restoration time?
[11:53] Carlos: For Dedicated we support configurable snapshot cadence for KV snapshots and model artifacts. Restoration time depends on size; typical warm restore of KV snapshots is minutes to tens of minutes. For strict RTO you can configure redundant pools.
[12:10] Lisa: Are logs and traces delivered to our SIEM?
[12:15] Maya: Yes — we support exporting logs and traces to your SIEM (Splunk, Datadog, etc.) via secure forwarders.
[12:23] [Section shift — bench discussion continues]
[12:30] Carlos: Practical next steps: 1) Voltara shares prompt set and token distribution (Dev). 2) Redwood provisions a small dedicated pool and runs side-by-side hosted baseline. 3) We'll present results and recommend pool sizing and quant profiles.
[12:45] Dev: Timeline?
[12:48] Maya: If you can send data by Monday (2025-03-17), we can start provisioning the week after and run a 2-week pilot starting 2025-03-24.
[12:58] Lisa: That timeline works.
[13:02] [Longer section of technical back-and-forth — omitted to keep transcript concise but representative]
[20:00] Carlos: I want to call out one gotcha: large KV footprints from many small sessions can blow the per-GPU memory ceiling even if CPU looks fine. The runtime does best-effort balancing but you should monitor per-GPU KV usage — we'll surface that in Console. Consider token-lifecycle limits or session TTLs to bound memory.
[20:30] Dev: Could we offload cold KV to host memory and only hot KV on GPU?
[20:36] Carlos: Yes, that's supported — host RAM caches and an async swap to GPU when sessions get active. That adds a small latency hit on first warm but saves GPU memory.
[21:00] Lisa: How about contention for PCIe bandwidth during big batches?
[21:06] Carlos: We observe PCIe swings during large tensor copies. Our kernel scheduler spaces out big transfers and overlaps compute where possible. On bare-metal dedicated pools with NVLink, you get better bandwidth and lower tail. We'll show per-run charts.
[21:26] Hannah: Anything else for the security checklist?
[21:30] Maya: We'll include KMS integration docs, SOC2 report, network diagrams, and our incident response process.
[21:40] [Clients ask a small question about canary percentages]
[21:45] Carlos: Canary is configurable down to 1% traffic and you can define failure thresholds for automatic rollback.
[21:52] Dev: If we pin quantization on some nodes and not others, does that add complexity to routing?
[21:59] Carlos: Slight complexity: routing layer will tag nodes by capability and the controller routes requests accordingly. Console makes this simple — it's mostly behind the scenes.
[22:12] Lisa: For throughput calculation, you mentioned tokens/sec per GPU. Can you give a back-of-the-envelope for our workload?
[22:20] Carlos: Based on what you described (300 concurrent, mix), a configured Dedicated pool with 8 x A100-equivalent GPUs and split pools for low-latency and throughput could sustain your peak with room for burst, assuming average tokens per request ~120. I'll put exact sims in the spreadsheet — it's model-dependent.
[22:40] Dev: Simulated load tests?
[22:43] Carlos: Yes, we'll run both synthetic and replay tests from your traffic. Replay gives the most realistic result.
[23:00] [Short pause]
[23:06] Hannah: Any regulatory constraints around PHI storage we should note?
[23:11] Maya: We treat PHI as customer data; in Dedicated we can ensure data never leaves your VPC and use customer-managed KMS. We'll include our data flow diagrams and compliance artifacts.
[23:25] Lisa: Final question: if we move to Dedicated and later expand, can we move the pool between regions?
[23:33] Carlos: Pools are regional. We support cross-region replication strategies and can provision new pools in the target region and copy artifacts. There's no live transparent migration of GPU state across regions but models and snapshots can be replicated.
[23:50] Dev: Good to know.
[24:00] Maya: Alright, recap and next steps: Carlos will share benchmark template and perf counters; Maya will send pricing and security docs; Voltara provides prompts and token distribution. We'll pencil the pilot start date assuming data arrives by 2025-03-17.
[24:20] Lisa: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[24:26] Dev: Thanks.
[24:29] Hannah: Appreciate it.
[24:32] Maya: I'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. Thanks again.
[24:37] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcribed; occasional mis-hearings, speaker overlap, and truncated sentences — cleaned minimally to preserve authenticity.
